subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: National Curriculum (KS2 geography: volcanoes, earthquakes, structure of the Earth, Europe case study); school AQA tectonics sequence used for subject knowledge

lessons.title: Inside the Earth: its layers
objectives: Name the four layers of the Earth
Describe the features of each layer
Explain why the Earth's crust is like the skin of an apple

keywords.def: the thin, hard outer layer of the Earth
the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust
the layer of very hot liquid metal around the centre
the solid, extremely hot ball of metal at the centre

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the stages of the water cycle.
What do you think is under our feet if we dig down deep enough?

teach.heading: A journey to the centre
bullets: The Earth is made of layers.
From outside to inside: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.
The deepest holes people have dug reach only the crust.
teach.note: Use a peach or an egg to model the layers: skin, flesh and stone (or shell, white and yolk). Ask children to predict which layer is the thickest. The deepest drill hole (the Kola Borehole in Russia) is about 12 km, which is tiny compared with the Earth's radius of about 6,400 km.

teach.heading: The crust
bullets: The crust is the thin outer layer where we live.
It is solid rock. It is between 5 and 70 km thick.
It is broken into huge pieces called plates.
teach.note: Compare the crust to the skin of an apple. Explain that it is thinnest under the oceans and thickest under big mountain ranges. Introduce the word plates only briefly; the next lesson will cover them in detail.

teach.heading: The mantle
bullets: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick.
It is very hot rock that moves slowly.
Parts of it are so hot they can melt into magma.
teach.note: The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows extremely slowly, a bit like very thick toffee over thousands of years. Magma is melted rock beneath the surface. When magma erupts onto the surface it is called lava. Check the difference.

teach.heading: The core
bullets: The outer core is liquid metal, mostly iron and nickel.
The inner core is solid metal and extremely hot.
It is over 5,000 degrees Celsius, as hot as the Sun's surface.
teach.note: The inner core is solid because the pressure is so great, even though it is hotter than the outer core. Ask children why a solid inner core might surprise us. Link: the temperature of the inner core is similar to the surface of the Sun.

practice: Put the four layers in order from the surface to the centre.
Match each layer to its description: thin and solid, thick and hot rock, liquid metal, solid metal ball.
independent: Draw and label a cross-section of the Earth showing all four layers.
Write one fact about each layer under your diagram.
Stretch: explain why the crust is the best layer for humans to live on.
exit: Name the four layers of the Earth in order.
lessons.homework: Make a model of the Earth's layers using playdough or draw an apple and label it as the Earth.
lessons.send: Provide a pre-drawn circle with sections to label. EAL: pre-teach crust, mantle, core with objects. Stretch: calculate the thickness of the layers and compare them in a bar chart.

lessons.title: Tectonic plates and the Ring of Fire
objectives: Explain that the Earth's crust is split into tectonic plates
Describe how plates move and meet
Locate the Ring of Fire on a world map

keywords.def: a huge slab of the Earth's crust that moves very slowly
a horseshoe-shaped area around the Pacific Ocean with many volcanoes and earthquakes

starter: Say Bismillah. Which layer of the Earth do we live on?
What is magma? How is it different from lava?

teach.heading: A cracked eggshell
bullets: The crust is broken into about seven large plates.
The plates fit together like a jigsaw.
They float on the hot mantle and move slowly.
teach.note: Crack a hard-boiled egg and show how the shell pieces fit. Show a map of the plates. The plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow, around 2 to 5 centimetres a year. Ask: would you notice? Not day to day, but over millions of years the continents have moved.

teach.heading: What happens at boundaries?
bullets: Plates can push together.
Plates can pull apart.
Plates can slide past each other.
teach.note: Demonstrate with your hands, pushing palms together, pulling apart, and sliding past. Relate each movement to a possible event: mountains and volcanoes where plates collide, new crust where plates part, earthquakes where plates slide. The idea 'movement causes events at the boundary' is the main point.

teach.heading: The Ring of Fire
bullets: The Ring of Fire circles the Pacific Ocean.
About three out of four volcanoes are in this ring.
Many earthquakes also happen here.
teach.note: Show a map with volcanoes and plate boundaries. Point out Japan, Indonesia, the Philippines, and the west coast of the Americas. About 75% of the world's active volcanoes are in the Ring of Fire. Ask why there are so many here (many plate boundaries). The UK is far from any plate boundary, which is why we rarely have big earthquakes.

teach.heading: Living near plate boundaries
bullets: Millions of people live near volcanoes and faults.
Fertile soil and geothermal energy help people.
Scientists watch the ground to warn people.
teach.note: Introduce the idea of risks and benefits. Volcanic soil is rich in minerals, so farmers grow crops. In Iceland hot water from underground heats homes. Ask pupils why people might live near a volcano despite the danger. Accept sensible reasons.

practice: On the world map, trace the Ring of Fire in red.
Act out: pushing together, pulling apart, sliding past. Say what could happen.
independent: Label a plate map: show the Pacific Plate, Eurasian Plate and African Plate.
Colour the Ring of Fire and name three countries on it.
Stretch: explain why the UK has fewer earthquakes than Japan.
exit: Name one place on the Ring of Fire.
lessons.homework: Find out one fact about earthquakes or volcanoes in Japan, Indonesia or Iceland and draw it.
lessons.send: Provide a map with plate boundaries marked in colour. EAL: use actions for push, pull and slide. Stretch: research the speed of plate movement and compare with growth of fingernails.

lessons.title: How a volcano works
objectives: Label the main parts of a volcano
Describe what comes out of a volcano

keywords.def: an opening in the Earth's crust where magma, ash and gas escape
the pipe or opening that magma travels up
the bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano
melted rock that has erupted onto the surface
a large pool of magma beneath a volcano

starter: Say Bismillah. What are tectonic plates?
What is the Ring of Fire?
What is the name of the hot melted rock under the ground?

teach.heading: Parts of a volcano
bullets: Magma collects in the magma chamber.
It rises up the vent.
It erupts from the crater at the top.
teach.note: Show a cross-section diagram. Trace the path of magma with a finger. Point to the main vent, side vent, crater, ash cloud and lava flow. Ask children to add each label as you go. Misconception: not all volcanoes are cone-shaped mountains; some are flat or under the sea.

teach.heading: Why does a volcano erupt?
bullets: Magma is lighter than the rock around it.
Gas dissolved in the magma pushes upwards.
Pressure builds until the volcano erupts.
teach.note: Shake a bottle of fizzy water and open the lid to show pressure released. This is a simple model of a gas-rich eruption. Make clear that this is only a model; the real thing involves hot rock. Do not do this indoors without precautions.

teach.heading: What comes out?
bullets: Lava, ash, gas and rocks.
Lava can be over 1,000 degrees Celsius.
Ash clouds can travel thousands of kilometres.
teach.note: Show photographs of a lava flow and an ash cloud. In 2010 the eruption of Eyjafjallajokull in Iceland sent ash across Europe and closed airspace for days. Ask children how that could affect aeroplanes and travel.

teach.heading: Active, dormant or extinct?
bullets: Active volcanoes erupt now or have recently.
Dormant volcanoes are sleeping but could erupt.
Extinct volcanoes will never erupt again.
teach.note: Ask children to match each word with an example: Mount Etna in Italy is active, Mount Fuji in Japan is classed as active but dormant, and Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh is extinct. Misconception: dormant does not mean safe forever.

practice: Label the parts of a volcano on a diagram: magma chamber, vent, crater, lava, ash cloud.
Sort these words: active, dormant, extinct. Match to the meaning.
independent: Draw and label a volcano before and during an eruption.
Write an eyewitness report of an eruption using at least four key words.
Stretch: explain why an ash cloud is dangerous for aeroplanes.
exit: What is the name of the hole at the top of a volcano?
What is the difference between magma and lava?
lessons.homework: With an adult's help, make a model volcano from paper or clay and label its parts.
lessons.send: Provide a diagram with labels to cut and stick. EAL: use gesture and picture cards for lava, ash and gas. Stretch: compare cone volcanoes with shield volcanoes.

lessons.title: Earthquakes and staying safe: Pompeii and Vesuvius
objectives: Describe what happened when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE
Say how people can stay safe in an earthquake or eruption

keywords.def: a sudden shaking of the ground
the point on the surface directly above where an earthquake begins
to leave a dangerous place and go somewhere safe

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the parts of a volcano.
What is the Ring of Fire?
What do you think we should do if the ground starts to shake?

teach.heading: What is an earthquake?
bullets: Plates can get stuck as they push past each other.
Pressure builds up and then rock suddenly slips.
The ground shakes. This is an earthquake.
teach.note: Use two rough pieces of sandpaper or two books pushed against each other until they suddenly slip. Explain that the point on the surface above the start is the epicentre. Ask: where would shaking be strongest? Near the epicentre.

teach.heading: Measuring earthquakes
bullets: A seismometer records shaking.
Scientists give each earthquake a number for its size.
Bigger numbers mean stronger earthquakes.
teach.note: Show a seismometer trace. The Richter and moment magnitude scales go from 1 to about 9. Each step up is much bigger. Do not go into the maths. Say that tiny earthquakes happen every day but most are too small to feel.

teach.heading: Vesuvius and Pompeii
bullets: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted in Italy.
The Roman town of Pompeii was buried under ash.
People and buildings were preserved for nearly 1,700 years.
teach.note: Show photographs of Pompeii today and of the casts of victims. Ask: what could scientists learn from the remains? They show us how Romans lived. Vesuvius sits near Naples; it is still an active volcano and today about 600,000 people live in the danger zone. Handle the photographs sensitively.

teach.heading: Staying safe
bullets: In an earthquake: drop, cover and hold on.
Stay away from windows and heavy objects.
For a volcano: follow evacuation plans and listen to warnings.
teach.note: Practise 'Drop, cover, hold on' with children under their desks or tables. Talk about how people prepare: emergency bags, practising drills and strong buildings. Remind children that Muslims trust in Allah and also take sensible precautions to keep themselves and others safe; keep this brief.

practice: Order the events of the Vesuvius eruption using pictures.
Practise the safety actions: Drop, Cover, Hold on. Say why each one helps.
independent: Make a safety poster for an earthquake with three clear rules.
Write a diary entry from a child in Pompeii on the day of the eruption.
Stretch: explain why a large earthquake in a poor country might cause more damage than in a rich country.
exit: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
Name one safety action in an earthquake.
lessons.homework: Make a family emergency plan: where is a safe spot in your home during an earthquake or fire?
lessons.send: Provide a poster template with symbols. EAL: use drill actions to teach vocabulary. Stretch: research the earthquake in Turkey and Syria in February 2023 and discuss why buildings collapsed.
